title: UnDercontrol File
description: An uploaded file, via 'ud apply -f'. Uses the YAML envelope format (apiVersion/kind/metadata/spec). A file is metadata plus bytes in object storage, and only the metadata is in this document — there is no field naming a local path, because a manifest describes the state a file should be in and a path that resolves on one machine is not part of that state. The bytes come from the call instead: 'ud apply --content-file <path>'. Identity is (owner, path, name), resolved by the CLI at apply time, so a document with no 'metadata.id' updates the file it names rather than creating a second one — unless two or more files already share that key, which 'spec.fileKey' breaks and which is otherwise refused. The kind is 'File' while the table, the API routes and the 'resource://' protocol are still called resource; the permission layer has called this concept file since day one (file:upload, file:read, file:delete).

metadata.description: 'metadata.id' names an existing file directly and takes precedence over the (path, name) key; a full UUID or an 8-character prefix. Omit it and the key decides. 'metadata.tags' is accepted as an alternative to 'spec.tags' — giving both is an error rather than a precedence rule, so the ignored one cannot look effective.

name.description: The file's name, including its extension — unlike a diagram, this really is a file and the extension is part of what it is. Together with 'path' it forms the identity a re-apply resolves against. It need not match the base name of '--content-file': the document names the file, the flag only says where the bytes are. The MIME type is derived from this name, so calling it 'report.pdf' stores it as a PDF whatever the local file was called.

path.description: Virtual folder the file appears under in the explorer tree. Part of the identity key: the same name under two folders is two files. Normalized before use with the same rules the server applies on write (unsafe characters become '-', leading and trailing dots, dashes and spaces are stripped), because the server's list filter compares paths with raw equality — an un-normalized path would match nothing and be read as 'no such file'. Omitting it and giving '/' mean the same folder.

fileKey.description: READ-ONLY. The storage key the file's bytes are under, written by 'ud describe file <id> -o apply' and never sent back to the server — a document cannot move a file's bytes by editing this. It is here because it is an IDENTITY: when two or more files share (path, name) it names which one this document means, which is the case 'ud apply' otherwise refuses. Replacing a file's content retires its key rather than deleting the object, so a key that no longer matches the current version is resolved against the file's stored versions and reported as 'version N of this file, superseded on <date>' — the document still applies to the CURRENT version, and apply never silently rolls content back. A fileKey matching neither the current version nor any stored one is an error, not a licence to fall back on guessing by (path, name).

tags.description: Tags for categorization. Applied as a whole list: applying a document with fewer tags removes the ones it leaves out, and an empty list clears them. Omit the field entirely to leave the file's tags alone. Mutually exclusive with 'metadata.tags'.

entity_type.description: Attach the new file to something as it is created — 'todolist' for a task. Note the entity type is the storage-level name: a task is a 'todolist' here, the same seam 'ud upload resource --entity-type' has. Only read on create; use the attachment endpoints to change it afterwards.

entity_id.description: The id of the entity named by 'entity_type'. A task id may be an 8-character prefix. Quote it: an all-digit short id is a YAML integer when bare.

identity_and_idempotency.description: (owner, path, name) is a CLI-side convention here, NOT a unique index — and it will not become one. 'ud upload resource' creates rows without checking for a duplicate name and legitimately does so every day; a unique index would start rejecting those uploads, which would be a change to the old path. So two files can share a key. 'spec.fileKey' breaks the tie when the document has one; without it 'ud apply' refuses such a document (printing the candidate ids) rather than guessing which row it means. Exporting with '-o apply' writes both 'metadata.id' and 'spec.fileKey', so a document that has been round-tripped once is immune to this.

idempotency_of_content.description: Applying the same document twice writes nothing: the key resolves to the existing file and every metadata field already matches, so no PATCH is issued. The bytes are not part of the document at all, so this is not a claim about them either way. To replace them, say so in the call: 'ud apply -f doc.yaml --content-file ./new.png' uploads unconditionally — no content hash is stored, so nothing can compare the local bytes with the stored ones, and re-running it replaces them with identical ones rather than detecting a match.

three_states_of_a_lookup.description: Resolving the identity key has three outcomes, and the CLI keeps them apart: the file is there, the file is definitely not there, or the lookup did not succeed (server unreachable, authentication failed). Only the second creates. Reporting a failed lookup as 'not found' would let a single network blip create a duplicate of a file that already exists, with no unique index to catch it.

storage_accounting.description: A file's bytes live in object storage and count against the storage quota, which is checked when the upload is prepared. Creating a file through 'ud apply --content-file' uses exactly the same prepare/upload/confirm path as 'ud upload resource', so it carries the same quota behaviour. Replacing content adds to the account rather than exchanging: the replaced version is kept and stays charged (see 'replacing_content'). Diagrams are exempt from the quota; files are not.

deprecated_kind.description: 'kind: Resource' is still accepted and behaves identically, with a deprecation warning. Older exports produced by 'ud describe resource <id> -o apply' use that form and keep working; new exports write 'kind: File'.

replacing_content.description: '--content-file' on a file that already exists replaces its bytes, and does so without ever writing over the bytes it is replacing: the new content goes to a NEW storage key, the server verifies that object really landed at the right size, and only then does the file's row move onto it. Every way an upload can fail — network, crash, truncation, an abandoned client — therefore ends with the file's current content untouched and still downloadable. The version that was replaced is kept, not deleted: it stays downloadable through 'ud describe file <id> --history' and it COUNTS AGAINST THE STORAGE QUOTA while it does. It appears in no file listing, so a file replaced five times can be holding six times its size with only one of them visible; 'ud delete file-version <id> <n>' is how that space is released.
